Some people argue that primary schools should abolish homework because young children need time to rest and play after school. While rest and play are certainly important, getting rid of homework altogether would be a mistake. Short, purposeful daily homework helps children practise essential skills, build good study habits, and keep parents connected to their learning. Rather than abolishing homework, schools should make sure it is manageable, meaningful, and suited to the age of the child.

One of the strongest reasons to keep homework in primary schools is that it reinforces the reading and arithmetic skills pupils learn in class. Children do not become confident readers or accurate mathematicians simply by hearing a lesson once. They improve through regular practice. For example, a child who reads for fifteen minutes each evening is likely to develop better fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension than a child who reads only during school hours. Similarly, practising times tables, number bonds, or simple problem-solving at home helps pupils remember methods and gain speed. These basic skills are like building blocks: if they are weak in primary school, children may struggle with more advanced work later.

Homework also helps children develop independent work habits that will be essential in secondary school. At primary level, a small daily task teaches pupils how to organise their time, follow instructions, and complete work without a teacher standing beside them. A child who learns to sit down, check what has been assigned, and finish a task carefully is developing responsibility and self-discipline. These habits become even more important in secondary school, where pupils must manage several subjects, meet deadlines, revise for tests, and complete longer assignments. Primary homework therefore acts as gentle preparation for the greater independence expected later.

In addition, homework gives parents a valuable window into what their child is studying. Without homework, many parents would know very little about the books their child is reading, the maths methods being taught, or the areas where their child may need help. A spelling list, reading record, or worksheet can start useful conversations at home and allow parents to encourage progress. For instance, if a parent notices that a child is struggling with subtraction, they can practise together or speak to the teacher before the problem grows.

For these reasons, primary schools should not abolish homework. When kept reasonable and focused, daily homework strengthens core skills, encourages independence, and builds an important link between home and school.

Primary schools should not abolish homework, because carefully planned daily practice plays an important role in children’s learning and development. While young pupils certainly need time to rest, play, and spend time with their families, a short and purposeful homework routine can strengthen what they learn in class and prepare them for future academic demands. Instead of removing homework altogether, schools should ensure that it is manageable, meaningful, and closely connected to classroom learning.

Daily homework is especially valuable for reinforcing reading and arithmetic skills. These are not abilities that children master simply by hearing a lesson once; they improve through repetition, confidence, and regular use. A child who reads for fifteen minutes each evening becomes more fluent, expands vocabulary, and develops better comprehension. Similarly, arithmetic skills such as number bonds, times tables, and basic problem-solving become quicker and more automatic when practised frequently. For example, a pupil who regularly completes a few multiplication questions at home is more likely to approach longer calculations in class with confidence. Homework therefore acts as a bridge between learning something new and remembering it well enough to use it independently.

Homework also helps children develop the independent work habits they will need when they move on to secondary school. In primary school, pupils are often closely guided by teachers throughout the day, but secondary school requires greater responsibility. Students must manage different subjects, meet deadlines, organise materials, and complete tasks without constant reminders. A simple daily homework routine teaches these habits gradually. Children learn to sit down, focus, follow instructions, and finish a task even when a teacher is not beside them. These skills are not only academic; they are life skills. If pupils enter secondary school having never been expected to work independently at home, the sudden increase in responsibility can be stressful and discouraging.

Homework is also a valuable way for parents to stay informed about what their child is studying. Many children give only brief answers when asked what they did at school, but homework provides a clear window into classroom learning. When parents hear their child read, check a maths worksheet, or discuss a spelling list, they can see both progress and difficulties. This allows them to offer encouragement and, when necessary, raise concerns with the teacher before small problems become serious gaps. Homework can therefore strengthen the partnership between home and school.

For these reasons, abolishing homework in primary schools would be a mistake. When it is reasonable in length and thoughtfully designed, daily homework reinforces essential skills, builds independence, and keeps parents connected to their child’s education. Rather than abandoning homework, schools should use it wisely.

Office jobs should default to remote work whenever the work can be done effectively outside a physical office. While in-person collaboration still has value for training, team-building, and certain creative sessions, making remote work the default would better reflect how many modern office tasks are actually performed: through email, shared documents, video meetings, project management platforms, and specialized software. A remote-first approach can improve employees’ lives, expand opportunities for employers, and reduce business costs.

One of the strongest arguments for remote work is the time employees reclaim by eliminating the daily commute. In many large metropolitan areas, workers spend an hour or more traveling to and from the office each day. According to U.S. Census data, the average one-way commute in the United States is close to 27 minutes, meaning many workers lose nearly five hours each week just getting to work. Remote work gives that time back. Employees can use it for exercise, childcare, cooking healthier meals, education, or rest—all of which can improve well-being and reduce burnout. Some employees may also choose to devote part of that time to focused work, allowing them to start the day earlier, prepare more thoroughly for meetings, or complete tasks without the stress of traffic or crowded transit. In this way, remote work can support both personal satisfaction and productivity.

Companies also benefit by removing geographic limits from hiring. A business based in New York, San Francisco, or London no longer needs to recruit only from people who live nearby or are willing to relocate. It can hire a skilled software engineer in a smaller city, a marketing specialist in another country, or a customer support manager in a region with different language skills and time-zone coverage. This broader talent pool helps companies find better matches for specialized roles and can improve diversity by opening doors to candidates who cannot move because of family, disability, housing costs, or immigration constraints.

Finally, remote work can create major financial advantages. Office space is expensive, especially in major business districts. Rent, utilities, maintenance, furniture, parking, security, and office supplies all represent significant overhead. If companies reduce their physical footprint through remote-first policies, those savings can be redirected toward higher salaries, better benefits, employee development, or research and development. For example, a company that downsizes from several floors of leased office space to a smaller collaboration hub could invest the difference in product innovation or competitive compensation.

Remote work is not perfect for every role, but for many office jobs it should be the default. It gives workers back valuable time, helps companies recruit more broadly, and frees resources for priorities that matter more than maintaining empty desks.

Office jobs should default to remote work because it offers major benefits to employees, employers, and the broader economy. While some tasks still require in-person collaboration, many knowledge-based roles can be performed effectively from anywhere. Making remote work the standard, rather than the exception, would save time, expand opportunity, and allow companies to use resources more efficiently.

One of the strongest arguments for remote work is the time employees regain by eliminating the daily commute. In many metropolitan areas, workers spend 30 minutes to an hour traveling each way. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the average one-way commute in the United States is roughly 27 minutes, meaning many full-time employees lose more than 200 hours per year just getting to and from work. Remote work gives that time back. Employees can use it for exercise, family responsibilities, rest, or education, all of which can improve well-being and reduce burnout. Some may also choose to spend part of that reclaimed time on work itself—starting earlier, answering messages thoughtfully, or completing focused tasks without the stress of traffic or crowded public transit. In this way, remote work can support both healthier lives and higher productivity.

Remote arrangements also help companies hire better candidates by removing geographic limits. A business based in New York, for example, no longer needs to recruit only from people willing to live within commuting distance of Manhattan. It can hire a skilled software engineer in Ohio, a marketing analyst in Texas, or a customer support specialist in rural Maine. This broader talent pool is especially valuable in competitive industries where specialized skills are scarce. It can also promote diversity by opening opportunities to people who cannot easily relocate, including caregivers, people with disabilities, military spouses, and workers in lower-cost regions.

The financial case for remote work is equally compelling. Office space is expensive, particularly in major cities. Rent, utilities, maintenance, furniture, parking, and office services can represent a significant share of overhead. If companies reduce their physical footprint through remote-first policies or occasional shared workspaces, they can redirect those savings toward higher salaries, better benefits, employee training, or research and development. For a technology company, savings from unused office floors could help fund new product development. For a nonprofit, the money might support additional staff or expanded services.

Remote work is not a cure-all, and companies must still invest in communication, cybersecurity, and team culture. However, for many office jobs, the advantages are clear. By defaulting to remote work, organizations can give employees back valuable time, hire from a wider and more diverse talent pool, and spend less on real estate while investing more in people and innovation.

Making urban public transport free for all users is often dismissed as an unrealistic luxury, but it should be understood instead as a practical investment in better cities. Public transport is not merely a service purchased by individual riders; it is infrastructure that supports the whole urban economy, reduces pressure on roads, and connects people to opportunity. Eliminating fares would bring benefits that extend far beyond those who step onto buses, trams, or trains.

One strong argument for free public transport is that fare collection itself is expensive. Transit agencies spend substantial sums on ticket machines, card systems, barriers, inspectors, software, administration, and enforcement. They must also manage disputes, penalties, maintenance of payment equipment, and the delays caused when passengers queue, tap, or struggle with malfunctioning systems. These costs do not move a single person any farther or faster. If fares were abolished, much of this money and staff time could be redirected toward what riders actually need: more frequent service, cleaner vehicles, safer stations, better accessibility, and expanded routes. A transport system designed around moving people rather than collecting payments would be simpler, faster, and more efficient.

Free public transport would also help reduce congestion. Many urban car journeys are short trips that could be made by bus, tram, or metro if doing so were easy and attractive. Fares may seem small, but for families, occasional riders, or people making multiple trips, they can make driving feel more convenient or economical. Removing fares changes that calculation. When public transport is free at the point of use, residents have a stronger incentive to leave the car at home, especially for errands, school runs, and local journeys. Even a modest reduction in car use can improve traffic flow, shorten travel times, reduce pollution, and make streets safer for pedestrians and cyclists.

Most importantly, fare-free transport would expand freedom for low-income residents. For people living on tight budgets, the cost of daily travel can be a serious barrier to finding work, attending appointments, reaching education, buying affordable groceries, or visiting family. Mobility is a condition of full participation in urban life. If cities want residents to take jobs, use public services, and contribute to their communities, they should not make basic movement prohibitively expensive. Free transit would function as a direct, practical form of support, giving people access to opportunities rather than leaving them isolated by cost.

Cities thrive when people can move easily, affordably, and efficiently. By eliminating fares, urban governments could reduce wasteful administrative costs, ease congestion, and promote social equity. Free public transport is not simply a giveaway; it is a smart public policy that would make cities fairer, cleaner, and more livable for everyone.

Making urban public transport free for all users is not merely a generous social policy; it is a practical investment in healthier, fairer, and more efficient cities. Fare-free transit would strengthen public transport systems, ease pressure on crowded streets, and expand opportunity for residents who depend most on affordable mobility. At a time when cities face rising inequality, congestion, and environmental strain, eliminating fares is a reform whose benefits would reach far beyond the bus or train.

One of the strongest arguments for free public transport is that fare collection itself is expensive. Transit agencies must pay for ticket machines, fare gates, card systems, inspectors, enforcement staff, maintenance, software, accounting, and the administration needed to manage payments and penalties. These costs can consume a significant share of the revenue fares are supposed to generate. In some systems, especially bus networks with lower fare recovery, the net financial benefit of charging passengers may be far smaller than it appears. If fares were eliminated, operators could redirect money and staff time toward what riders actually need: more frequent service, cleaner vehicles, better shelters, improved accessibility, and safer stations. Free boarding would also speed up buses by removing delays caused by payment, making service more reliable for everyone.

Free public transport would also help cities reduce traffic congestion. Many urban car journeys are short trips that could be made by bus, tram, or metro if public transport were convenient and costless at the point of use. Fares may seem small, but for families, occasional riders, and people comparing a quick car trip with a paid transit journey, they can discourage use. Removing that barrier would make public transport the obvious choice for more daily errands, school runs, and commutes. Even a modest shift away from private cars would reduce the number of vehicles competing for limited road space, cutting delays, noise, and pollution. Streets would become more efficient and more pleasant for pedestrians, cyclists, and local businesses.

Most importantly, fare-free transit would expand freedom for low-income residents. For people living paycheck to paycheck, the cost of daily travel can determine whether they can accept a job, attend a medical appointment, visit a government office, or buy groceries at a cheaper store. Mobility is not a luxury; it is a condition for full participation in city life. By removing fares, cities would connect residents to employment, education, healthcare, and community resources without forcing them to choose between transport and other necessities.

Free urban public transport is therefore a policy of economic sense and social justice. It would reduce wasteful fare-collection costs, encourage less car dependence, and give every resident greater access to the opportunities cities promise.

A decarbonised electricity system must do more than produce clean energy on average: it must deliver power reliably, affordably, and at the scale modern societies require. For that reason, nuclear power is an indispensable complement to renewables. While wind and solar are essential to cutting emissions, their output varies with weather, season, and time of day. Nuclear plants, by contrast, provide firm, dispatchable or near-continuous generation with high capacity factors—often above 80–90% in leading fleets, according to the International Energy Agency and World Nuclear Association. Technical studies of deep decarbonisation, including work by the IPCC and systems-modeling research in journals such as *Joule* and *Energy Policy*, consistently find that low-carbon grids become harder and more expensive to balance when they rely exclusively on variable renewables. Nuclear power reduces the need for extreme overbuilding, long-duration storage, and fossil backup, thereby strengthening grid reliability.

Nuclear energy is also firmly within the category of low-carbon electricity when assessed across its full lifecycle. Lifecycle analysis accounts not only for plant operation but also mining, construction, fuel processing, and decommissioning. The IPCC’s comparative estimates place nuclear power’s median lifecycle emissions at roughly 12 gCO₂-eq/kWh, comparable to wind and lower than solar photovoltaics in many assessments, while far below gas and coal. The UNECE and other technical reviews similarly conclude that nuclear’s emissions are among the lowest of any commercial electricity source. This matters because climate policy should be guided by total system emissions, not by misleading impressions about individual technologies. A nuclear plant may be complex to build, but once operating it generates vast quantities of electricity for decades with minimal direct carbon output.

Land use further strengthens the case for nuclear. Because uranium fuel is extraordinarily energy-dense, nuclear facilities produce large amounts of electricity from compact sites. By contrast, wind and solar farms require much larger areas to collect diffuse natural energy flows, even when dual land use is possible. Studies by the U.S. National Renewable Energy Laboratory and others show that utility-scale solar and wind typically require orders of magnitude more land per unit of firm annual electricity than nuclear stations. In densely populated or ecologically sensitive regions, this spatial efficiency is not a minor advantage: it reduces pressure on habitats, agriculture, transmission expansion, and local opposition.

A realistic clean-energy strategy should therefore combine the strengths of technologies rather than force a false choice between them. Renewables can supply abundant low-cost electricity when conditions are favorable; nuclear can provide the stable, low-carbon backbone that keeps the system dependable. If the goal is rapid, durable decarbonisation, excluding nuclear power would make the task harder, riskier, and more land-intensive.

A decarbonised electricity system must do more than generate clean power; it must generate clean power reliably, at scale, and with tolerable demands on land and materials. For that reason, nuclear energy should be regarded not as a rival to renewables, but as an indispensable complement to them. Technical assessments by the International Energy Agency, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, and numerous electricity-system modelling studies show that deep decarbonisation becomes harder, costlier, and riskier when firm low-carbon generation is excluded. Nuclear power provides precisely that: large volumes of dispatchable, low-carbon electricity available in all seasons and weather conditions.

First, nuclear power’s greatest system value is its ability to provide stable output independent of meteorology. Wind and solar are essential technologies, but their production varies with wind speeds, daylight, cloud cover, and seasonal patterns. This intermittency can be managed with grids, storage, demand response, and overbuilding, but those solutions become increasingly expensive at very high renewable shares. Nuclear plants, by contrast, operate at high capacity factors—often above 80–90% in well-run fleets—and can supply continuous electricity through periods of low wind and solar output. The technical literature on “firm low-carbon resources,” including studies by Sepulveda et al. and analyses from the IEA, consistently finds that systems combining variable renewables with firm clean generation are more resilient and often cheaper than systems relying on renewables and storage alone.

Second, nuclear power has lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions comparable to the best low-carbon technologies. While reactor construction, uranium mining, fuel processing, and decommissioning all produce emissions, these are spread over immense quantities of electricity generated across many decades. IPCC lifecycle estimates commonly place nuclear at roughly 12 gCO₂-equivalent per kWh, similar to wind and below most solar photovoltaic estimates, depending on manufacturing conditions and location. This is dramatically lower than coal and gas, even when gas is used in efficient combined-cycle plants. The relevant comparison, therefore, is not whether nuclear is literally zero-emission, but whether it belongs in the portfolio of technologies capable of displacing fossil fuels at scale. On lifecycle evidence, it clearly does.

Third, nuclear power has a major advantage in land use. Because uranium has extremely high energy density and reactors produce large amounts of electricity from compact sites, nuclear installations require far less land per unit of energy than wind or solar farms. Wind projects can coexist with agriculture, and solar can be deployed on rooftops and degraded land, but utility-scale renewable buildouts still require extensive spatial planning, transmission expansion, and public consent. Nuclear plants concentrate generation on relatively small sites, often near existing grid infrastructure. In densely populated countries, or regions with competing demands for land, this spatial efficiency is a decisive benefit.

A credible clean-energy strategy should use every tool that can cut emissions quickly and reliably. Wind, solar, storage, transmission, efficiency, and demand flexibility are all vital. But excluding nuclear power removes one of the few proven sources of firm, large-scale, low-carbon electricity. A decarbonised grid that includes nuclear is more dependable, land-efficient, and technically robust than one that tries to manage the climate challenge without it.

Universities should not abandon standardised tests as a factor in admissions decisions. While no test is perfect and no single measure should determine a student’s future, a common assessment can play an important role in making admissions fairer, more transparent, and more accurate. Used alongside grades, essays, recommendations, and contextual information, standardised tests help universities compare applicants who come from very different educational circumstances.

First, a common standardised test provides a level playing field for students from diverse schools and regions. High schools vary widely in curriculum, grading standards, course difficulty, teacher expectations, and available resources. An “A” at one school may not represent the same level of preparation as an “A” at another. A standardised test gives all applicants at least one shared measure, taken under broadly similar conditions and scored by the same criteria. This can be especially valuable for students from lesser-known schools, rural areas, or international systems, whose academic records may be harder for admissions officers to interpret. A strong test score can signal ability even when a student’s school lacks advanced courses or a long history of sending graduates to selective universities.

Second, eliminating standardised tests could worsen existing inequalities in admissions. Without a common metric, universities would rely more heavily on factors that often reflect privilege: polished application essays, prestigious extracurricular activities, costly enrichment programmes, unpaid internships, legacy connections, and recommendations from well-resourced schools. Wealthier students are more likely to have access to private counsellors, essay coaches, and impressive résumé-building opportunities. By contrast, a standardised test, though influenced by preparation and resources, is still a relatively direct academic measure. If universities are concerned about inequality, the better solution is not to remove tests entirely, but to interpret scores in context and expand access to free preparation and fee waivers.

Third, standardised tests have demonstrated predictive validity, particularly when used with high school grades. Grades are useful indicators of persistence, classroom performance, and long-term effort, but they are affected by grade inflation and inconsistent standards across schools. Standardised tests measure core academic skills such as reading, mathematical reasoning, and problem-solving, which are relevant to university-level work. Research has often found that test scores and high school grades together predict first-year university performance better than either measure alone. Therefore, abandoning tests would remove information that can help identify students likely to succeed, especially when grades alone are difficult to compare.

For these reasons, universities should retain standardised tests as one factor in holistic admissions. The goal should be fair use, not total abandonment.

Universities should not abandon standardised tests in admissions. While no single measure can capture a student’s full potential, a common standardised test remains an important tool for fairness, consistency, and academic prediction. Used alongside grades, essays, recommendations, and context, it helps admissions officers compare applicants more accurately and reduces the risk that decisions will depend too heavily on unequal school environments.

First, a standardised test provides a common yardstick for students from widely different educational backgrounds. High schools vary enormously in course difficulty, grading standards, teacher expectations, and available academic resources. An “A” at one school may represent mastery of advanced material, while the same grade at another may reflect less rigorous coursework or grade inflation. A shared assessment gives every applicant the opportunity to demonstrate core academic skills under the same conditions. This does not mean the test is perfect or that scores should be viewed without context, but it does mean that universities gain an additional piece of comparable evidence when evaluating students from thousands of schools.

Second, eliminating standardised tests could actually worsen existing inequalities in admissions. Without test scores, universities would likely place more weight on factors such as extracurricular activities, personal essays, recommendation letters, advanced coursework, and school reputation. These measures are often even more influenced by privilege. Wealthier students may have access to private admissions consultants, expensive enrichment programs, unpaid internships, and well-connected recommenders. Students from under-resourced schools may have fewer Advanced Placement courses, larger class sizes, and less guidance in preparing application materials. A standardised test can help identify talented students who might otherwise be overlooked because their schools cannot offer the same opportunities as affluent institutions.

Third, standardised tests have meaningful predictive value, especially when combined with high school grades. Grades are useful indicators of effort, persistence, and performance over time, but they are not uniform across schools. Standardised test scores, by contrast, measure academic preparation in a consistent way. Research has often found that both grades and test scores predict first-year university performance, and that the combination of the two is stronger than either measure alone. In other words, the test should not replace high school grades, but it can supplement them by helping universities forecast which students are prepared for college-level work.

For these reasons, universities should improve the use of standardised tests rather than discard them. A fair admissions system should consider context, but it should also preserve common measures that promote comparability and help uncover potential across diverse backgrounds.

A four-day working week should be adopted as national policy because it offers a practical way to improve productivity, health and employment at the same time. For too long, working culture has confused time spent at a desk with real economic value. Modern economies depend increasingly on focus, creativity, organisation and technology, not simply on the number of hours employees are physically present. A shorter week would recognise this reality and encourage employers to design work more intelligently.

Trials of the four-day week have repeatedly shown that employees can maintain their output even when working fewer hours. When people know they have less time to complete their tasks, they tend to reduce unnecessary meetings, avoid distractions and prioritise important work. Many companies that have tested shorter weeks have reported stable or even improved productivity, not because staff are working harder in an unhealthy way, but because work becomes more efficient. A national policy would push organisations to measure results rather than attendance, rewarding effectiveness instead of presenteeism.

A better-rested workforce would also take less sick leave. Long working weeks contribute to stress, burnout, poor sleep and preventable illness, all of which impose costs on employers, health services and families. Giving workers an extra day to recover, exercise, attend appointments, care for relatives or simply rest would improve both mental and physical health. Employees who return to work refreshed are more alert, more motivated and less likely to make mistakes. Fewer absences would help businesses plan more reliably and would reduce the hidden economic damage caused by exhaustion.

A four-day week would also help create more jobs by spreading available work across more people. If national policy encouraged shorter full-time schedules, some employers would need additional staff to cover opening hours, customer service, production or public services. This could reduce unemployment and underemployment, particularly for young people, parents, carers and those seeking more flexible entry into the labour market. Instead of concentrating excessive hours among some workers while others struggle to find secure employment, society could distribute paid work more fairly.

Adopting a four-day working week would not mean abandoning ambition or weakening the economy. It would mean building a smarter, healthier and more inclusive labour market. By maintaining output, reducing sickness and widening access to employment, a shorter working week offers benefits for workers, businesses and the country as a whole. National policy should now catch up with the evidence and make the four-day week a serious standard for the future.

A four-day working week should be adopted as national policy because it offers a practical way to improve people’s lives while strengthening the economy. For too long, working culture has treated long hours as proof of commitment, even when those hours do not produce better results. A shorter week would recognise a simple truth: productivity depends not only on time spent at work, but on energy, focus and motivation. If introduced carefully, with protections for pay and staffing, a four-day week could become one of the most important social and economic reforms of our time.

Trials in several countries and industries have shown that employees can maintain, and sometimes even increase, their output while working fewer hours. When the working week is shortened, organisations are encouraged to reduce pointless meetings, improve planning, use technology more intelligently and focus on the work that actually matters. Employees, knowing they have less time, often become more disciplined and efficient. The result is not a loss of productivity, but a better use of working time. National policy should support this shift because it would push businesses away from outdated habits and towards smarter, more productive working practices.

A better-rested workforce would also take less sick leave. Stress, exhaustion and burnout are major causes of absence, and they are often made worse by a five-day week that leaves too little time for family, exercise, medical appointments, sleep and recovery. Giving people an extra day away from work would help them manage their health before problems become serious. It would also improve mental wellbeing, which is increasingly important in modern workplaces. Fewer sick days would benefit employers as well as workers, reducing disruption and the costs associated with absence.

A shorter working week could also help create more jobs by spreading available work across more people. In sectors where demand cannot simply be compressed into four days, employers would need additional staff to cover opening hours and maintain services. This could provide opportunities for unemployed people, young workers and those seeking part-time roles. Instead of concentrating work among overstretched employees while others struggle to find secure employment, society could distribute work more fairly.

Adopting a four-day working week would not be a reckless experiment, but a forward-looking response to evidence. It would promote productivity, improve health and share opportunity more widely. National policy should help make it the new standard.

Mandatory age verification for social media is often presented as a simple solution to a serious problem: protecting minors from online harm. But while the goal is legitimate, the policy is deeply flawed. Requiring every user to prove their age would create major privacy risks, fail to reliably keep minors off platforms, and place unequal burdens on vulnerable groups. Rather than making the internet safer, mandatory age verification could make it less private, less accessible, and no more effective at protecting young people.

First, age verification threatens individual privacy on a large scale. To confirm a user’s age, platforms may require government identification, facial scans, credit card information, or third-party identity checks. This means social media companies—or verification vendors—would collect and store sensitive personal data from millions of users. Such databases would be attractive targets for hackers and could expose people to identity theft, stalking, or surveillance. Even if companies promise not to misuse the information, history shows that data collected for one purpose is often repurposed, shared, or breached. Users should not have to surrender highly sensitive personal information simply to participate in ordinary online conversation.

Second, mandatory age verification may not actually prevent minors from accessing social media. Determined young users can borrow a parent’s identification, use another person’s account, rely on VPNs, or move to less regulated platforms. Strict verification rules may push minors away from mainstream sites, where there are at least some moderation systems and reporting tools, and toward more obscure or unsafe online spaces. A policy that is easy to evade by the people it targets but invasive for everyone else is not a strong solution.

Third, mandatory verification would not affect all users equally. People without current government identification, stable housing, credit cards, or reliable technology could be locked out of online platforms. This includes low-income individuals, undocumented people, young adults, elderly users, and those living in rural areas. For many, social media is not merely entertainment; it is a way to access news, community support, job opportunities, political organizing, and emergency information. A system that conditions access on formal identification risks excluding the very people who already face barriers to participation in public life.

Protecting minors online requires better tools: stronger privacy settings by default, improved content moderation, digital literacy education, parental controls, and enforcement against exploitative design. Mandatory age verification offers the appearance of action while creating serious harms. A safer internet should not be built by forcing everyone to sacrifice privacy and access.

Mandatory age verification for social media accounts is often presented as a simple solution to a serious problem: protecting children from online harm. But while the goal is important, the policy is deeply flawed. Requiring every user to prove their age would create major risks to privacy, would likely fail to keep determined minors off platforms, and would place unequal burdens on people who already face barriers to digital access.

First, mandatory age verification would require users to hand over sensitive personal information, such as government identification, facial scans, credit card details, or other records. This would create large databases of highly valuable personal data. Even if companies promise to protect that information, data breaches are common, and social media platforms do not have a perfect record of safeguarding users’ privacy. A system designed to protect children could instead expose millions of people—including minors—to identity theft, surveillance, and misuse of personal information. It would also reduce online anonymity, which many people rely on to discuss sensitive topics such as health, sexuality, politics, religion, or abuse.

Second, age verification is unlikely to be fully effective. Young people have always found ways around digital restrictions, whether by using a parent’s account, borrowing someone else’s identification, using virtual private networks, or moving to less regulated platforms. A strict verification system may push minors away from mainstream services that have moderation tools and reporting systems and toward more obscure or unsafe corners of the internet. In that case, the policy could make children harder to protect, not safer.

Third, mandatory verification would not affect everyone equally. People without government-issued identification, stable housing, credit cards, or reliable access to technology may be excluded from social media altogether. This could disproportionately harm low-income users, undocumented immigrants, elderly people, survivors of domestic violence, and others who may be unable or unwilling to submit identifying documents. For many, social media is not merely entertainment; it is a tool for education, community, work, organizing, and emergency communication.

A better approach would focus on privacy-preserving safety measures: stronger content moderation, better parental tools, digital literacy education, default privacy protections for young users, and accountability for platforms that promote harmful content. Protecting minors online is essential, but mandatory age verification is a blunt instrument. It threatens privacy, offers only limited effectiveness, and risks excluding vulnerable groups. Safety should not come at the cost of fundamental rights and equal access to the digital public square.

The argument that a significant portion of space-exploration funding should be redirected to ocean research rests on a misleading assumption: that these two areas draw from a single, interchangeable pool of money. In reality, the budgets, institutions, objectives, and political coalitions behind space and ocean science are often quite distinct. Space programmes are frequently funded through agencies with mandates tied not only to science, but also to national security, telecommunications, weather forecasting, technological competitiveness, and international prestige. Ocean research, by contrast, is commonly supported through environmental, fisheries, climate, geological, or academic funding streams. Cutting space exploration would not automatically produce a proportional increase in oceanographic budgets; the money might simply be absorbed elsewhere or never appropriated at all. The more persuasive case is not to weaken one scientific enterprise in order to support another, but to argue directly for stronger ocean funding on its own merits.

Moreover, the supposed opposition between space research and ocean research ignores how deeply the two are already connected. Satellite observation is one of the most powerful tools oceanographers possess. From orbit, satellites measure sea-surface temperature, ocean height, wave patterns, ice extent, salinity, chlorophyll concentrations, storm formation, and the movement of major currents. These observations are indispensable for climate science, hurricane prediction, fisheries management, coral reef monitoring, and tracking oil spills and harmful algal blooms. No network of ships, buoys, or underwater vehicles can provide the same continuous global coverage. In this sense, investment in space capabilities directly strengthens our ability to understand and protect the oceans. Redirecting funds away from space systems could therefore harm, rather than help, marine science by reducing the very infrastructure on which modern ocean observation depends.

Finally, space programmes have an unusually high capacity to generate benefits far outside their immediate mission. Because space exploration demands extreme reliability, miniaturisation, advanced materials, robotics, navigation, communications, energy storage, and data processing, it drives innovation in technologies that later spread into medicine, manufacturing, agriculture, disaster response, computing, and environmental monitoring. The economic and scientific spillovers from space investment are broad, long-lasting, and often unpredictable. This does not mean ocean research is unimportant; indeed, it is vital. But the case for funding it should not be built on diminishing space exploration, one of the most productive engines of technological development. A wiser policy would expand support for ocean science while preserving the space programmes that already serve both Earth science and wider society.

The argument that a significant portion of space-exploration funding should be redirected to ocean research rests on a misleading assumption: that these two areas draw from a single, easily transferable pool of money. In practice, space and ocean science are usually funded through different agencies, legislative priorities, strategic mandates, and international partnerships. Space budgets often support national security infrastructure, communications, weather forecasting, launch capability, and long-term technological development, while ocean research funding is commonly tied to environmental agencies, fisheries management, climate monitoring, and marine conservation. Cutting space programmes would not automatically produce a corresponding increase in ocean research; the money might simply be absorbed elsewhere or lost in broader budget negotiations. If ocean science is underfunded, the more direct and honest solution is to increase its own funding rather than weaken a separate scientific enterprise whose purposes and institutional foundations are different.

Moreover, space research is not an alternative to ocean research but one of its most powerful enablers. Satellites are indispensable for understanding the oceans at a planetary scale. They measure sea-surface temperatures, sea-level rise, ocean colour, salinity, currents, ice cover, storm formation, and the spread of pollutants or algal blooms. No fleet of research vessels, however well funded, could continuously monitor the entire surface of the Earth’s oceans with the breadth, consistency, and frequency provided by orbital instruments. Climate science in particular depends on long-term satellite records, because the oceans regulate heat, carbon, and weather systems across the globe. Redirecting funds away from space observation could therefore weaken ocean science rather than strengthen it. The deep sea still requires ships, submersibles, sensors, and biological sampling, but those tools complement satellite systems; they do not replace them. A serious commitment to ocean research should recognize that space infrastructure is part of the ocean-observation network.

Finally, space programmes have an unusually strong record of producing benefits far beyond their original missions. The demands of operating in space drive advances in materials science, robotics, miniaturized electronics, solar power, telecommunications, navigation, medical imaging, water purification, software, and remote sensing. These spillovers diffuse into commercial industries, public services, disaster response, agriculture, transport, and environmental monitoring. Space exploration also sustains highly skilled supply chains and pushes engineering capabilities that are difficult to generate through less demanding projects. Ocean research is unquestionably valuable and deserves robust support, but it does not follow that space exploration should be treated as the bill-payer. A wiser policy would fund both, recognizing that space science not only expands human knowledge outward but also supplies tools, technologies, and economic returns that help us manage problems here on Earth, including those in the oceans themselves.

A society that treats digital payment as the inevitable replacement for cash mistakes convenience for completeness. Electronic transfers, cards, and mobile wallets are efficient when the systems beneath them are functioning, but they depend on a dense infrastructure of electricity, telecommunications, banking networks, payment processors, and devices. Cash is different: it works at the point of exchange without a signal, a server, or a charged battery. During power outages, cyber incidents, natural disasters, or network failures, physical money can keep basic commerce alive, allowing people to buy food, fuel, medicine, and transport when digital rails are unavailable. Maintaining a robust circulation of cash is therefore not nostalgia; it is a form of civic resilience, much like keeping emergency supplies or backup generators. A payments system that lacks a non-digital fallback is efficient only until the moment it becomes fragile.

Cash also possesses a characteristic that no mainstream digital payment method can truly replicate: it allows a transaction to occur without automatically producing a permanent, traceable record. This anonymity is not merely a convenience for those wishing to hide wrongdoing; it is a legitimate feature of personal freedom. People may have many lawful reasons to keep purchases private, including medical needs, political donations, religious materials, personal relationships, or simple preference. In a digital economy, every transaction can become data: recorded, analysed, sold, hacked, subpoenaed, or used to profile behaviour. Cash preserves a zone of ordinary privacy in daily life, limiting the extent to which participation in commerce requires surrendering personal information. A democratic society should be cautious about making every purchase visible by default.

Most importantly, cash remains essential for people who are not well served by digital finance. The unbanked may lack access to accounts, stable addresses, identification documents, affordable internet, or trust in financial institutions. Many elderly people, meanwhile, may struggle with smartphones, passwords, fraud risks, small screens, or rapidly changing payment technologies. For these groups, cash is not an outdated preference but a practical necessity that enables independence and inclusion. If shops, services, and public institutions abandon cash, they effectively exclude citizens who are already vulnerable. Preserving cash circulation ensures that the economy remains accessible to all, not only to those who are digitally connected, financially integrated, and technologically confident. In that sense, cash is more than money: it is a public instrument of resilience, privacy, and fairness.

A society that depends entirely on digital payments is a society that assumes its invisible infrastructure will always work. Yet power cuts, network failures, cyberattacks, software outages, and natural disasters can instantly turn a seamless payment system into a locked door. In such moments, physical cash becomes more than a nostalgic convenience; it is a form of public resilience. A banknote does not need a charged battery, a functioning card terminal, a mobile signal, or a remote server to approve it. When storms disable electricity, when payment networks go down, or when local businesses lose connectivity, cash allows people to keep buying food, fuel, medicine, and transport. Maintaining a robust circulation of cash is therefore not resistance to innovation, but prudent contingency planning. Just as communities keep emergency supplies and backup generators, economies need a payment instrument that continues to function when the digital layer fails.

Cash also has a distinctive civic value because it is the only widely accepted payment method that does not automatically create a transactional record. Most electronic payments leave trails: where a person was, what they bought, when they bought it, and sometimes with whom. While such data can support convenience and fraud prevention, it also raises questions about surveillance, profiling, data breaches, and the gradual normalization of constant monitoring. The ability to make lawful purchases without being tracked is part of personal privacy, not evidence of wrongdoing. People may wish to buy a medical item, donate to a cause, purchase a gift, or manage their daily affairs without generating permanent data points. Cash preserves a zone of anonymity in ordinary life, helping ensure that participation in the economy does not require surrendering a detailed map of one’s habits and movements.

Most importantly, cash remains indispensable for people whom digital finance does not adequately serve. The unbanked may lack formal identification, stable housing, regular income, internet access, or trust in financial institutions; for them, cards and mobile wallets are not simple alternatives but barriers. Many elderly people also rely on cash because it is familiar, tangible, and easier to budget with than abstract balances on screens. Some may struggle with smartphones, passwords, fraud risks, or inaccessible banking interfaces. If cash disappears, these groups do not become effortlessly digital; they become more excluded. A fair payments system must serve the whole public, not only the connected, banked, and technologically confident. Preserving cash therefore protects resilience, privacy, and inclusion alike.

Proposals to phase out zoos often arise from an understandable concern for animal welfare, but they overlook the vital role that well-regulated modern zoos now play in global conservation. The strongest argument against abolishing them is that many zoos are no longer merely places of display; they are centres of survival for species pushed to the edge by habitat loss, poaching, disease and climate change. Carefully managed breeding programmes have helped prevent the disappearance of animals such as the Arabian oryx, the California condor, the black-footed ferret and the Przewalski’s horse. These successes did not happen by accident. They required international cooperation, genetic record-keeping, specialist husbandry and long-term planning. Without captive assurance populations, some species would have vanished before their habitats could be protected or restored. To phase out zoos entirely would be to remove one of the few practical safeguards available for animals already facing extinction.

Zoos also provide something that documentaries, books and online campaigns cannot fully replace: direct emotional contact between people and living animals. Conservation depends not only on scientific knowledge but also on public will, and people are far more likely to support protection efforts when they have seen, heard and felt a connection with the creatures at risk. A child who watches a gorilla interact with its family, or an adult who comes face to face with an endangered tiger, may leave with a deeper sense of responsibility than any statistic could inspire. Modern zoos can turn curiosity into commitment by linking exhibits to education, fundraising and practical conservation campaigns. If society becomes physically and emotionally distant from wildlife, conservation risks becoming an abstract cause rather than a shared moral duty.

In addition, veterinary research conducted in zoos has produced major benefits for animals in the wild. Zoo veterinarians develop techniques for treating injuries, managing infectious diseases, improving nutrition, understanding reproduction and safely anesthetising large or fragile species. This knowledge is often transferred directly to field conservation, where wild populations may need vaccination, rescue, rehabilitation or disease monitoring. Research on captive animals can also help scientists respond more effectively to crises, from fungal infections in amphibians to reproductive difficulties in endangered mammals. Rather than phasing out zoos, we should demand high standards, close poor institutions and strengthen those that contribute meaningfully to conservation. Abolishing zoos would satisfy a simple slogan, but it would weaken a complex and necessary network that many endangered species still depend on.

The idea that every child should be taught programming from the age of six sounds modern and forward-looking, but it is not the best use of children’s earliest years in school. Young children do benefit from learning how to think logically, solve problems, and use technology responsibly. However, making programming a universal requirement at such an early age risks crowding out the learning experiences that matter most for healthy intellectual and social development. Before children are asked to write code, they need time to build the broad foundations that make later learning possible.

The early years of education are more effectively spent developing language, number sense, and imaginative play. Reading, speaking, listening, and storytelling help children understand the world, express themselves, and communicate with others. A strong grasp of numbers, patterns, and quantities prepares them for mathematics far more deeply than memorising commands on a screen. Imaginative play is also not a luxury; it is one of the ways children develop creativity, empathy, self-control, and flexible thinking. These are the very qualities that later make someone a good problem-solver, whether in science, art, business, or technology. If six-year-olds spend too much structured time on coding lessons, they may lose opportunities to explore language, movement, social interaction, and make-believe in ways that are more suitable for their stage of development.

Another problem is that programming tools and technologies change extremely quickly. A child who learns a particular coding platform or simplified language at six may find that it is outdated long before they are old enough to use programming in a meaningful professional or academic setting. Of course, some basic computational ideas can last, but these can be taught through puzzles, games, mathematics, and creative activities without requiring formal programming instruction. Schools should be cautious about presenting early coding as an essential future skill when the specific tools children learn may soon disappear. It is better to teach adaptable thinking later, when students have stronger literacy, numeracy, and abstract reasoning skills.

Finally, the shortage of qualified teachers makes universal early coding instruction unrealistic. Many schools already struggle to recruit specialists in mathematics, science, and computing. Expecting every primary school to deliver high-quality programming lessons to every six-year-old would place a heavy burden on teachers who may not have the training, confidence, or resources to do it well. Poorly taught coding could become frustrating, superficial, and unequal, benefiting children in well-resourced schools while leaving others behind. Rather than forcing programming into every early classroom, education systems should first strengthen the essentials and introduce coding later, when schools can teach it properly and children are ready to benefit from it.

Proposals to phase out zoos often begin from a humane impulse: a belief that wild animals belong in the wild. Yet this argument overlooks the reality that many wild habitats are shrinking, fragmented, polluted, or threatened by poaching and climate change. In this context, well-regulated modern zoos are not relics of entertainment but essential conservation institutions. Their breeding programmes have helped prevent the disappearance of numerous species that might otherwise have vanished forever. Species such as the Arabian oryx, the California condor, the black-footed ferret, and Przewalski’s horse have all benefited from carefully managed captive breeding and reintroduction efforts. These programmes maintain genetic diversity, provide insurance populations against catastrophe, and create the possibility of restoring animals to protected habitats when conditions improve. To abolish zoos would be to remove one of the few practical safeguards available to species already on the edge.

Modern zoos also perform a role that documentaries, books, and online campaigns cannot fully replace: they bring people into direct contact with living animals. Seeing an elephant’s intelligence, a tiger’s power, or a frog’s fragility can turn abstract concern into emotional commitment. Conservation depends not only on scientific knowledge but on public support, funding, political pressure, and changes in behaviour. People are more likely to protect what they have encountered and come to value. For many children, especially those in cities or without the means to travel, a zoo may be the first place where the natural world feels real rather than remote. If society loses these encounters, conservation risks becoming an issue understood by specialists but ignored by the wider public whose backing is essential.

Zoos are also centres of veterinary research that benefit animals far beyond their gates. The close observation and medical care possible in zoos have advanced knowledge of wildlife nutrition, reproduction, disease, anaesthesia, injury treatment, and neonatal care. Techniques developed with zoo animals can later be used in field conservation, helping veterinarians treat endangered species, manage outbreaks, and improve survival rates in reintroduction programmes. Research into diseases affecting amphibians, great apes, birds, and large mammals often depends on expertise built in zoological institutions. Phasing out zoos would weaken this network of practical knowledge at precisely the moment wild populations face growing health threats. Rather than abolish zoos, we should demand high standards, strong welfare rules, and a clear conservation mission, because responsible modern zoos remain vital allies in protecting the planet’s most vulnerable species.

The idea that every child should be taught programming from the age of six may sound forward-looking, but it risks misunderstanding what young children need most. The early years of education are a crucial period for building the foundations on which all later learning depends: language, number sense, social confidence, and imaginative play. A six-year-old benefits enormously from learning to read with understanding, speak clearly, listen carefully, count confidently, recognize patterns, and explore ideas through stories, games, art, and physical activity. These are not “soft” alternatives to technical skills; they are the roots of flexible thinking. Imaginative play, in particular, helps children develop creativity, cooperation, problem-solving, and emotional awareness. If programming is introduced too early as a universal requirement, it may crowd out richer and more age-appropriate experiences that support the whole child.

Another problem is that programming tools and technologies change at extraordinary speed. The languages, platforms, and methods that seem essential today may be far less relevant by the time a six-year-old reaches adolescence or adulthood. Teaching very young children specific coding skills can therefore create a false sense of preparation. What will matter more in the long run is not whether a child learned a particular programming environment in primary school, but whether that child can think logically, communicate ideas, adapt to new information, and learn independently. These habits can be cultivated through mathematics, reading, puzzles, science exploration, and creative projects without requiring formal coding instruction at such an early age. It is wiser to introduce programming later, when students have the maturity and foundational knowledge to understand it more deeply and apply it more meaningfully.

Finally, making programming compulsory for all six-year-olds ignores a practical reality: many schools do not have enough qualified teachers to provide high-quality coding instruction. Good programming education is not simply a matter of placing children in front of screens or handing teachers a scripted app. It requires instructors who understand both computing concepts and child development. In many places, schools already struggle to recruit teachers for core subjects, support students with diverse needs, and provide basic resources. Requiring universal early coding instruction could widen inequalities, because wealthier schools would hire specialists while under-resourced schools would offer shallow or poorly supported lessons. Rather than imposing an unrealistic mandate, education systems should focus first on strong foundational learning and introduce programming later, thoughtfully and equitably.

Banning private cars from city centres is one of the most effective steps a city can take to become healthier, more efficient, and more economically vibrant. The private car is an extraordinarily space-intensive way to move people through dense urban areas: a single vehicle often carries one person while occupying road space, kerb space, junction capacity, and parking areas that could serve many more people if used differently. City centres are not primarily places for high-speed vehicle movement; they are places of work, shopping, culture, public life, and social exchange. Removing private cars therefore aligns the use of urban space with the real purpose of central districts.

The most immediate benefit is the liberation of street space. Roads and parking lanes currently devoted to private vehicles can be converted into wide pedestrian thoroughfares, protected cycle tracks, bus lanes, trees, seating, terraces, market stalls, and public squares. This does not merely make streets more attractive; it makes them function better. Walking becomes safer and more pleasant, cycling becomes a practical option for a wider range of people, and public transport is less delayed by congestion. Commercial activity also gains from a better public realm: cafés can spill outdoors, shops become easier to browse, and streets become destinations rather than corridors to be hurried through. In dense city centres, reallocating space from cars to people is a more productive use of scarce land.

The environmental gains are also rapid and measurable. Evidence from low-traffic zones, pedestrianised centres, and car-restricted districts shows that air quality can improve within weeks or months, especially through reductions in nitrogen dioxide and particulate pollution associated with traffic. Noise pollution also falls sharply when engines, acceleration, braking, and horn use are removed from central streets. These changes matter because air pollution is linked to asthma, heart disease, and premature death, while chronic noise contributes to stress, sleep disruption, and poorer mental health. A car ban is therefore not just an aesthetic intervention; it is a public health measure whose benefits can appear quickly after implementation.

Nor does the economic case against car bans withstand scrutiny. Although some retailers fear that fewer cars mean fewer customers, many cities that restrict private vehicles find the opposite: footfall rises. This is because most central shoppers arrive by public transport, bicycle, or on foot, and they are more likely to linger in safe, attractive streets. Pedestrian environments encourage browsing, repeat visits, and outdoor spending. By making city centres cleaner, calmer, and more enjoyable, car bans can strengthen rather than weaken urban commerce. Far from excluding people, they create places where more people want to be.

Banning private cars from city centres is one of the most effective ways to reclaim urban space for the people who actually use and sustain cities. Private vehicles are an extraordinarily inefficient use of scarce land: they carry relatively few people while requiring wide carriageways, junctions, parking bays, and access lanes that dominate public space. Once cars are removed, streets can be redesigned as pedestrian thoroughfares, protected cycle routes, pocket parks, outdoor seating areas, delivery zones, and spaces for markets or cultural events. This is not merely an aesthetic improvement; it changes how a city functions. Walking becomes safer and more pleasant, cycling becomes a practical option for a wider range of residents, and public transport can move more reliably when it is no longer trapped behind private traffic. The result is a centre that is more accessible, not less, because it prioritises movement by many people over storage and movement of relatively few cars.

The environmental gains are also immediate and measurable. Evidence from low-traffic and car-restricted schemes in cities such as Madrid, Oslo, Paris, and London shows that reductions in vehicle access can produce rapid improvements in air quality, particularly in nitrogen dioxide and particulate pollution associated with road traffic. Madrid Central, for example, was followed by notable falls in roadside nitrogen dioxide, while London’s traffic-reduction and ultra-low-emission policies have been associated with significant pollution reductions in affected areas. Noise pollution also falls quickly, because traffic is the dominant source of urban noise in many city centres. Fewer engines, horns, accelerations, and braking events mean streets become calmer within days, not decades. These improvements matter for public health: cleaner air reduces respiratory and cardiovascular risks, while quieter streets lower stress, improve sleep, and make public spaces more comfortable for conversation, work, and leisure.

Nor does the policy damage city-centre commerce in the way opponents often predict. The fear is that if customers cannot drive directly to shopfronts, they will stop coming. In practice, many cities find the opposite: retail footfall rises when streets become safer, cleaner, and more attractive places to spend time. Pedestrians and cyclists may buy less per visit than drivers, but they tend to visit more often, and car-free environments encourage lingering, browsing, café use, and spontaneous purchases. Businesses benefit from wider pavements, outdoor dining, improved visibility, and a more relaxed public realm. Far from emptying city centres, car bans can make them destinations again: places to walk, meet, shop, and enjoy, rather than corridors of congestion to be endured.

El trabajo a distancia debería convertirse en la modalidad habitual para los empleos de oficina, no como una concesión excepcional, sino como una forma más racional de organizar la vida laboral. La experiencia reciente ha demostrado que muchas tareas administrativas, creativas, técnicas y de gestión pueden realizarse con eficacia desde cualquier lugar, siempre que existan objetivos claros, herramientas adecuadas y una cultura basada en la responsabilidad. Frente al modelo tradicional centrado en la presencia física, el teletrabajo ofrece ventajas concretas para los trabajadores, las empresas y la sociedad.

En primer lugar, elimina o reduce de manera significativa el tiempo destinado a los desplazamientos diarios. Millones de personas invierten cada semana varias horas en ir y volver de la oficina, a menudo en condiciones de tráfico, estrés o transporte público saturado. Ese tiempo podría emplearse de forma mucho más valiosa: comenzar antes una tarea compleja, formarse en nuevas habilidades, hacer ejercicio, descansar mejor o compartir más momentos con la familia. No se trata solo de comodidad, sino de productividad y bienestar. Un trabajador que no inicia la jornada agotado por un trayecto largo tiene más posibilidades de concentrarse, rendir mejor y mantener una relación más saludable con su empleo.

Además, el trabajo remoto amplía enormemente el acceso de las empresas al talento. Cuando una organización exige presencia diaria en una ciudad concreta, limita su búsqueda a quienes viven cerca o pueden mudarse. En cambio, si acepta empleados a distancia, puede contratar a profesionales cualificados de distintas regiones e incluso países. Esto favorece equipos más diversos, con experiencias y perspectivas variadas, y permite cubrir puestos especializados que quizá serían difíciles de encontrar en el mercado local. Para las empresas, competir por talento ya no debería depender tanto de la ubicación de sus oficinas, sino de la calidad de sus proyectos y condiciones laborales.

Por último, el teletrabajo permite reducir costes asociados al alquiler, mantenimiento, mobiliario, suministros y servicios de grandes espacios de oficina. Esos recursos pueden reorientarse hacia fines más productivos: mejores salarios, programas de formación, herramientas tecnológicas, innovación o investigación y desarrollo. Una empresa que gasta menos en metros cuadrados puede invertir más en las personas y en las ideas que realmente generan valor.

Adoptar el trabajo a distancia como norma no implica eliminar toda interacción presencial. Pueden mantenerse reuniones puntuales o encuentros estratégicos cuando aporten valor. Pero para la mayoría de empleos de oficina, convertirlo en la modalidad habitual es una decisión eficiente, moderna y humana.

El trabajo a distancia debería convertirse en la modalidad habitual para los empleos de oficina, no como una concesión excepcional, sino como una evolución lógica de la vida laboral contemporánea. La tecnología ya permite realizar reuniones, coordinar proyectos, compartir documentos y evaluar resultados sin necesidad de coincidir físicamente en un mismo edificio. Si el objetivo de una empresa es producir con calidad y eficiencia, lo relevante no debería ser dónde se sienta un empleado, sino qué aporta y cómo cumple sus responsabilidades.

Uno de los beneficios más evidentes del teletrabajo es la eliminación o reducción de los desplazamientos diarios. Millones de personas pierden cada semana horas en transporte público o en atascos, tiempo que rara vez aporta valor a la empresa o al trabajador. Convertir esos trayectos en tiempo disponible permite iniciar la jornada con más energía, dedicar unos minutos a la planificación, formarse en nuevas habilidades o atender tareas personales básicas que reducen el estrés. También favorece una vida más equilibrada: hacer ejercicio, desayunar con la familia o descansar adecuadamente no son lujos, sino condiciones que mejoran la concentración y la salud. Un trabajador menos agotado suele ser más productivo y tomar mejores decisiones.

Además, el trabajo remoto amplía enormemente el acceso de las empresas al talento. Cuando una compañía exige presencia diaria en una ciudad concreta, limita su búsqueda a quienes viven allí o están dispuestos a mudarse. En cambio, al contratar a distancia, puede elegir entre profesionales cualificados de distintas regiones e incluso países. Esto aumenta la probabilidad de encontrar perfiles especializados, mejora la diversidad de perspectivas y permite formar equipos más sólidos. Para muchas organizaciones, especialmente las que compiten por talento técnico, creativo o analítico, esta apertura geográfica puede marcar la diferencia entre crecer o quedarse atrás.

A ello se suma una ventaja económica considerable: la reducción de los costes asociados al espacio de oficina. Al necesitar menos metros cuadrados, las empresas pueden ahorrar en alquileres, mantenimiento, mobiliario, electricidad y otros gastos fijos. Esos recursos no tienen por qué convertirse solo en beneficio contable; pueden reinvertirse en mejores salarios, programas de bienestar, capacitación o investigación y desarrollo. Una empresa que remunera mejor y que innova más resulta más competitiva y atractiva.

Por supuesto, el teletrabajo exige buena organización, comunicación clara y criterios de evaluación basados en resultados. Pero esos retos son manejables y, en muchos casos, obligan a las empresas a gestionar mejor. Por sus beneficios para los trabajadores, para las compañías y para la eficiencia general, el trabajo a distancia debería ser la norma en los empleos de oficina.

En los últimos años, muchas familias y centros educativos se han preguntado si conviene eliminar las tareas para casa en la educación primaria. Es cierto que una carga excesiva de deberes puede generar cansancio y restar tiempo al juego, al descanso y a la vida familiar. Sin embargo, eliminar por completo las tareas no parece la mejor solución. Lo razonable es mantenerlas, siempre que sean adecuadas a la edad de los niños, tengan un propósito claro y no ocupen demasiado tiempo.

En primer lugar, las tareas ayudan a consolidar los conocimientos adquiridos en el aula. En clase, los alumnos aprenden contenidos nuevos, pero no siempre basta con escucharlos o practicarlos una sola vez. Para que un niño domine una operación matemática, mejore su lectura o escriba con mayor claridad, necesita repetir, aplicar y revisar lo aprendido. Un ejercicio breve en casa puede servir para detectar dudas que en el aula pasaron desapercibidas. Además, permite que el alumno gane confianza: cuando comprueba que puede resolver una actividad por sí mismo, se siente más seguro y motivado.

En segundo lugar, las tareas preparan a los alumnos para la educación secundaria. En esa etapa, los estudiantes deben organizarse mejor, estudiar con más autonomía y asumir responsabilidades personales. Si durante la primaria nunca han tenido que planificar una pequeña actividad en casa, el cambio puede resultarles brusco. En cambio, unas tareas moderadas enseñan hábitos muy valiosos: anotar lo que deben hacer, distribuir el tiempo, cuidar la presentación y entregar un trabajo en la fecha prevista. Estas habilidades no se adquieren de un día para otro; se entrenan poco a poco.

Por último, los deberes también favorecen la implicación de los padres en el aprendizaje de sus hijos. No se trata de que los adultos hagan las tareas por ellos, sino de que conozcan qué están aprendiendo, qué dificultades tienen y cómo pueden acompañarlos. Leer juntos diez minutos, revisar una explicación o interesarse por una actividad escolar crea un puente entre la familia y la escuela. Esa comunicación beneficia al niño, porque siente que su educación importa tanto en clase como en casa.

Por todo ello, las tareas en primaria no deben desaparecer, sino ajustarse mejor. Deben ser breves, útiles y equilibradas. Bien planteadas, refuerzan aprendizajes, fomentan la responsabilidad y acercan a las familias al proceso educativo.

**La gratuidad del transporte público urbano: una inversión para ciudades más justas y eficientes**

El transporte público urbano cumple una función esencial en la vida cotidiana de las ciudades: permite el desplazamiento de millones de personas hacia sus trabajos, centros educativos, servicios de salud y espacios de recreación. Sin embargo, cuando su acceso depende del pago de una tarifa, se generan barreras económicas y costos administrativos que limitan su potencial. Por ello, la gratuidad del transporte público debe entenderse no solo como una medida social, sino también como una estrategia económica, ambiental y urbana.

En primer lugar, eliminar el cobro de tarifas podría reducir ciertos costos operativos asociados a la recaudación. Los sistemas actuales requieren infraestructura tecnológica, torniquetes, validadores, tarjetas, mantenimiento, personal de control, fiscalización y procesos administrativos vinculados al pago. Aunque la gratuidad no elimina los costos principales del servicio —como salarios, combustible, energía o mantenimiento de vehículos— sí puede simplificar la operación. Al no existir barreras de acceso ni tiempos de validación, el abordaje de pasajeros puede ser más rápido, lo que mejora la eficiencia del sistema y reduce demoras. En este sentido, parte de los recursos destinados a cobrar podrían redirigirse a mejorar frecuencias, ampliar rutas o renovar flotas.

En segundo lugar, la gratuidad puede modificar positivamente los patrones de movilidad urbana. Muchas personas utilizan el automóvil para trayectos cortos no porque sea la opción más eficiente, sino por comodidad o porque el costo del transporte público resulta poco atractivo frente al uso del vehículo ya disponible. Si el transporte público fuera gratuito, aumentaría su competitividad para desplazamientos breves, especialmente en zonas densas. Esto podría reducir la cantidad de viajes cortos en automóvil, que son particularmente ineficientes y contribuyen de manera significativa a la congestión.
